primitives.name: Lusin's Theorem
primitives.verbatim_quote: In the general case, there exists a sequence {fn} of simple functions converging to f; by Egoroff's theorem and the regularity of μ, there exists a compact set Co in E such that μ(E) ≦ μ(Co) + and such that {fn} converges to f uniformly on Co.
primitives.assumptions: Egoroff's theorem assumes a finite measure space. Regularity of μ ensures outer approximations by compact sets.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Failure occurs when uniform convergence fails on any compact subset, typically on non-compact domains.

primitives.name: Positive Linear Functional
primitives.verbatim_quote: A linear functional Λ on & is positive if Λ(f) ≥ 0 for every f in &+.
primitives.assumptions: Linearity requires additivity and homogeneity. Positivity restricts the range to non-negative reals.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Violates positivity when Λ(f) < 0 for some f ≥ 0, leading to signed measures or unbounded operators.

Positive linear functionals preserve order, enabling integration as a positive functional. Regularity connects contents to Borel measures, ensuring finite approximations. Monotonicity follows directly from positivity, forming the basis for dominated convergence and duality theory. These primitives interlock: Lusin's theorem uses regularity, while monotonicity underpins the Riesz representation theorem. Their failure modes highlight pathological behaviors in non-locally compact spaces or singular measures.
